Short Questions
Work Effectively within Bangladesh TVET Sector
Q1. What are four key features of the National Skills Development Policy?
Answer guide: Any four: NTVQF; CBT&A; Quality Assurance System; the role
of industry sectors in skills development; competent and certified
instructors/trainers; flexible institutional management; apprenticeship; RPL;
access for underprivileged groups; and labour-market information.
Q2. What type of information is included in a range statement?
Answer guide: A range statement may include applicable legislation (such as
OSH), tools, equipment, processes and procedures, special characteristics and
needs of learner groups, location, and the application of work under the quality-
assurance system.
Q3. How does RPL support learners and the training system?
Answer guide: RPL recognises skills and knowledge gained previously. It reduces
unnecessary retraining, saves time and cost, and helps determine training based on
skill gaps.
Q4. What are three objectives of a quality assurance framework?
Answer guide: Any three: ensuring institutions meet specified quality criteria;
ensuring fair and equitable services; improving qualification portability and
recognition; and applying credible assessment standards consistently.
Q5. What are the main functions of the NSDA?
Answer guide: Coordinating skills-development activities and linkages;
maintaining sector-based skills information; monitoring relevant skills-
development projects; and overseeing national competency, qualification and
quality-assurance arrangements.
Q6. List five candidate needs that may require consideration in competency
assessment.
Answer guide: Any five: language, literacy or numeracy needs; physical or
intellectual disability; learning progress; mental or psychological condition; prior
education and experience; religious or cultural considerations; age, gender,
motivation or location.

Q7. Give three reasonable-adjustment strategies for an older candidate.
Answer guide: Any three: read printed information aloud; use a sufficiently large
font; recognise the candidate's experience; allow adequate time; or use several
shorter assessment sessions instead of one long session.
Q8. What provisions can support access for people with disabilities?
Answer guide: Provide ramps or height-adjustable desks; large-print or Braille
materials; audio or assistive technology; and an interpreter or scribe as needed.
Q9. What strategies may support candidates in the gender category?
Answer guide: Where appropriate, provide an assessor of a suitable gender;
consider situations involving mixed-gender work; and schedule assessments
flexibly to accommodate childcare responsibilities.
Q10. Define workplace hazard and list four hazard types.
Answer guide: A hazard is a source or situation that can cause harm or injury.
Four types are physical, biological, chemical and ergonomic hazards.
Q11. List the steps of the hazard-management process.
Answer guide: Identify hazards; assess risks; apply controls; and review the
results.
Q12. What is the hierarchy of controls from bottom to top?
Answer guide: From lowest to highest: PPE → administrative controls →
engineering controls → isolation → substitution → elimination.
Q13. What is the importance of a worker's Right to Refuse?
Answer guide: A worker may refuse work they believe is unsafe. This protects
them from potential harm and supports a safer workplace.
Q14. List four causes of workplace accidents.
Answer guide: Any four: lack of hazard awareness; ignoring safety; not knowing
the correct safety procedures; poor housekeeping; inadequate lighting or
ventilation; incorrect use of tools; or unsafe conditions.
Q15. What are a supervisor's OSH responsibilities toward workers?
Answer guide: Be available to workers; answer their questions; provide feedback;
give hands-on training until work is performed correctly and safely; and monitor
safe work practices, including PPE use.

Q16. List four factors contributing to high injury rates among industrial workers.
Answer guide: Any four: inadequate training or experience; lack of awareness of
legal rights; fear of asking questions; and fatigue from work, study or other
responsibilities.
Q17. What are possible health effects of biological hazards?
Answer guide: Biological hazards may cause diseases or infections, allergies or
asthma, skin, eye or ear infections, colds or flu, and foodborne illness.
Q18. What tool can be used to define and classify the likelihood and consequences
of a risk?
Answer guide: A risk-analysis checklist.
Q19. Name three items of personal protective equipment relevant to your
occupation.
Answer guide: Any three items appropriate to the occupation, such as a safety
helmet, gloves, safety shoes, goggles or ear protection.
Q20. How do you add bullets to a paragraph in MS Word?
Answer guide: Select the paragraph, then choose Bullets in the Paragraph group
on the Home tab.
Q21. Explain how to merge cells in an MS Word table.
Answer guide: Select the cells, right-click and choose Merge Cells, or use Merge
Cells on Table Tools > Layout.
Q22. What is the difference between a worksheet and a workbook?
Answer guide: A workbook is a spreadsheet file; a worksheet is an individual
spreadsheet or page within that workbook.
Q23. What is the difference between animation and transition in PowerPoint?
Answer guide: Animation effects apply to text or objects within a slide; a
transition is the effect used when moving from one slide to another.
Q24. What are key points of time-management skills?
Answer guide: Meet deadlines; prioritise tasks; minimise distractions; allocate
suitable time to each task; and finish work within the agreed timeline.
Q25. Why is it important to assess all four dimensions of competency?
Answer guide: It shows whether a person can perform a specific task, manage
multiple tasks, respond to unexpected situations, and work within workplace roles
and relationships.

Q26. What do task-management skills involve?
Answer guide: Planning and coordinating multiple tasks to achieve a complete
work outcome, often while handling several tasks at the same time.
Q27. What do job/role environment skills involve?
Answer guide: Meeting workplace duties and expectations and interacting
effectively with managers, supervisors, colleagues, customers or suppliers.
Q28. What is contingency management skill?
Answer guide: The ability to respond effectively when errors, breakdowns or
unexpected situations disrupt normal work.
Q29. What is a competency standard?
Answer guide: An industry-defined performance specification that identifies the
skills, knowledge and attitudes required to work effectively in the workplace.
Q30. Why is it important for a TVET trainer to maintain technical competency?
Answer guide: The source question is incomplete: it is merged with the following
MCQ and provides no specific answer. The wording should be checked against the
original paper.
Q31. What is an element of competency?
Answer guide: A basic task or function within a unit of competency. It describes a
task that can be performed as part of a broader job or role.
Q32. Why should an assessor assess a candidate's contingency-management skills?
Answer guide: It helps determine whether a candidate can solve problems, make
decisions and adapt to irregularities, breakdowns and unexpected challenges.
Q33. What should a trainer consider when carrying out a task analysis?
Answer guide: Prioritise safety; define quality standards; provide appropriate
detail; use clear language; include hints or tips; and add visual aids such as
diagrams or photos when useful.
Q34. What is the difference between "must know" and "should know"
information?
Answer guide: "Must know" information is essential to achieve the task or
learning outcome. "Should know" information provides useful additional context
but is not always essential to complete the task.

Q35. Why should feedback be specific rather than general?
Answer guide: Specific feedback helps candidates understand what they did well
and what they need to improve, avoiding vague praise or criticism.
Q36. What are effective ways of giving feedback?
Answer guide: Ask candidates to assess their own performance first; identify
positive aspects; give specific praise; and explain corrective actions for
improvement.
Q37. Why should assessment feedback be given promptly?
Answer guide: Delayed feedback can allow misunderstandings to persist and
weaken the link between feedback and the work. Candidates may also forget their
thought process.
Q38. What is the difference between formative and summative assessment?
Answer guide: Formative assessment gives feedback on progress and
improvement during learning; summative assessment determines achievement or
competence at the end of a defined period.
Q39. What are the stages of preparing an assessment plan?
Answer guide: Review and understand the unit of competency; select elements;
identify evidence requirements (performance criteria, competency dimensions,
underpinning knowledge and skills, and critical aspects); select evidence-gathering
methods; and document the assessment/evidence plan.
Q40. What are performance criteria?
Answer guide: Performance criteria specify the standard of performance that must
be achieved to be considered competent.
Q41. What is an observation checklist?
Answer guide: A tool that structures the assessor's observations and records the
candidate's observable performance.
Q42. What is the purpose of an observation checklist in assessment?
Answer guide: To systematically observe, assess and record the observable steps
or performance demonstrated during a specific task.

Q43. What are the steps in designing competency-based assessment for a unit or
qualification?
Answer guide: Determine the competency standard and purpose/context; identify
evidence requirements; select assessment methods and instruments; identify
resources and equipment; document the plan and obtain stakeholder endorsement;
and prepare instruments and administrative documents.
Q44. What is the difference between assessment criteria and performance criteria?
Answer guide: Both describe expected performance. "Performance criteria" is the
term used in industry competency standards; "assessment criteria" specify the
performance learners must demonstrate to achieve a learning outcome.
Q45. What are the rules of evidence?
Answer guide: Validity, sufficiency, authenticity and currency. Some papers also
mention consistency, which is generally associated with reliability.
Q46. What must an assessor check before making a decision about collected
evidence?
Answer guide: Check whether evidence is valid, sufficient, current and authentic;
consistent across sources; and covers all relevant criteria and competency
dimensions.
Q47. What procedures can help establish authenticity of evidence?
Answer guide: Observe the work in progress; obtain a candidate declaration;
check drafts or work processes; and seek supervisor, employer or third-party
validation.
Q48. What are the requirements of valid evidence?
Answer guide: Evidence must cover all relevant elements and performance
criteria, competency dimensions, essential skills and knowledge or critical
evidence in the evidence guide, and mandatory conditions in the range statement.
Q49. What is an assessment benchmark?
Answer guide: The relevant industry competency standards are the benchmark.
For example, an OSH assessment in the food industry should use the applicable
food-industry standards.
Q50. How can reliability be improved in assessment? Give three points.
Answer guide: Any three: assess all candidates consistently; give clear and
consistent instructions; use a good guide for observation and judgment; and review
the tool regularly.

Q51. What is the difference between validity and sufficiency of evidence?
Answer guide: Validity means evidence is relevant to the current standards and
criteria. Sufficiency means there is enough varied evidence to cover all elements
and competency dimensions.
Q52. What is an assessment instrument?
Answer guide: An assessment instrument is a specific question, task or activity
used to collect evidence. An assessment tool also includes instructions for
collecting and interpreting evidence.
Q53. When is oral questioning useful in assessment?
Answer guide: Oral questioning is useful when observation is not possible, to
verify observations, to test underpinning knowledge, or to explore competency
dimensions such as contingency management and problem-solving.
Q54. What is competency-based assessment? Give four characteristics.
Answer guide: Any four: it is evidence-based and criterion-referenced; results are
generally Competent or Not Yet Competent; it focuses on workplace performance
standards; it is flexible and participatory; and evidence may be collected over time.
Q55. How should an assessor decide whether a candidate is competent?
Answer guide: Compare the candidate's evidence with the relevant performance
criteria and standards, taking competency dimensions and the rules of evidence
into account.
Q56. What does the evidence guide contain?
Answer guide: Relevant items include critical aspects of competency;
underpinning knowledge and skills; required attitudes; resource implications;
assessment methods; and context of assessment.
Q57. What should be considered when choosing assessment methods?
Answer guide: Consider the competency to be assessed; purpose and nature;
available resources; existing workplace evidence; usability of the tool; time and
cost; opportunities to collect realistic integrated evidence; and reasonable-
adjustment needs.
Q58. What should an assessor ask when evaluating evidence?
Answer guide: Is the evidence relevant and valid? Is it accurate? Is it the
candidate's own work and authentic? Is it consistent with other evidence? Is it
sufficient and current?

Q59. What does "failing to observe" mean as an assessor error?
Answer guide: Failing to notice an important point or cue because of insufficient
experience or preparation, especially when assessing many trainees.
Q60. What information should candidates receive before an assessment event?
Answer guide: Explain the assessment purpose; the unit being assessed; evidence
requirements; evidence-gathering methods; assessment conditions; and the
assessor's role.
Q61. What is free consent in assessment?
Answer guide: The candidate gives voluntary consent after understanding the
assessment context, purpose, procedures and legal/ethical responsibilities. They
must not be pressured to participate.
Q62. What are an assessor's ethical responsibilities?
Answer guide: Meet OSH requirements; keep assessment outcomes confidential;
obtain the candidate's informed consent; follow the organisation's quality policies
and procedures; and identify and responsibly manage conflicts of interest.
Q63. What is conflict of interest in assessment?
Answer guide: A situation in which an assessor's personal or professional
relationship or interest could affect impartial judgment. It should be disclosed and
managed appropriately.
Q64. Why is fairness an essential assessment principle?
Answer guide: Fairness gives every candidate an equitable, unbiased opportunity
and allows reasonable adjustments and appeal rights when needed, without
lowering competency standards.
Q65. What are four common errors made by assessors?
Answer guide: Examples include failing to observe, halo effect, horn effect,
failing to record, and overlooking cheating.
Q66. What should an assessor do if workplace production is affected by
assessment?
Answer guide: If assessment disrupts workplace operations, pause it and arrange
to resume at a suitable time or under suitable conditions.

Q67. Explain the two forms of evidence used in competency assessment.
Answer guide: Direct evidence is observed firsthand by the assessor, such as
performing a task or demonstration. Indirect evidence is obtained by reviewing
work products or other records, such as a finished product, written test, prior work
or testimonial.
Q68. Define assessment criteria.
Answer guide: Assessment criteria are the specific performance standards a
learner must meet to achieve a learning outcome or demonstrate competency.
Q69. What information does an assessment plan contain?
Answer guide: An assessment plan contains the purpose and context; personnel;
competency standards or benchmarks; assessment methods and tools; evidence
plan; organisational arrangements; physical and material resources; equipment;
and logistics.
Q70. What are two benefits of clustering competencies when designing assessment?
Answer guide: Any two: clustering reflects real work; gathers evidence for
several competency dimensions in one assessment; and uses assessment time and
resources efficiently.
Q71. What is Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) in competency-based
assessment?
Answer guide: RPL assesses skills and knowledge gained through prior work,
education or training against current standards, regardless of where or when the
learning occurred.
Q72. What are four characteristics of competency-based assessment?
Answer guide: Any four: evidence-based; criterion-referenced; uses
Competent/Not Yet Competent judgments; focuses on workplace performance;
and is flexible and participatory with reasonable adjustment.
Q73. What are the assessor's responsibilities for recording and retaining
assessment evidence?
Answer guide: Keep observation checklists, oral question sheets, written tests,
registration and self-assessment forms, result sheets, project/specification sheets
and other assessment records securely.

Q74. What is assessment recording and reporting?
Answer guide: Recording means documenting assessment results. Reporting
means communicating the outcome to an appropriate person, such as an
administrator, assessment-centre manager or employer.
Q75. What is competency assessment result summary (CARS)?
Answer guide: A concise summary of assessment outcomes showing which
competencies were assessed, which criteria were met and where improvement is
needed.
Q76. What are some sources for identifying workplace hazards?
Answer guide: Previous incidents or accidents; workers' feedback; workplace
inspections; reviews of equipment/material safety instructions; brainstorming;
legislation, standards or checklists; and advice from external consultants.
Q77. What are a candidate's ethical responsibilities during assessment?
Answer guide: Meet OSH requirements; keep assessment outcomes confidential;
provide full consent; and follow workplace quality systems, policies and
procedures.
Q78. How should the assessor ensure evidence is authentic?
Answer guide: Observe the candidate's work; obtain a declaration; check drafts or
work in progress; and use third-party validation when needed. Confirm that the
submitted work is the candidate's own and directly attributable to them.
Q79. What are the steps for deciding Competent or Not Yet Competent?
Answer guide: Compare evidence with the performance criteria; check the rules
of evidence and competency dimensions; then document the judgment.
Q80. What are four examples of indirect evidence?
Answer guide: Any four: assessment of a finished product; a written test of
underpinning knowledge; review of prior work; an employer/supervisor
testimonial; or training evidence.
Q81. What are the six points in an assessment agreement/process briefing?
Answer guide: The paper refers to six points but does not provide a specific list.
A typical briefing covers purpose/context, process/method, evidence/criteria,
timing/conditions, candidate rights/adjustment/appeal, and consent/recording.

Q82. How should the assessor handle a conflict of interest?
Answer guide: Identify and disclose the potential relationship or interest, then
follow the organisation's or NSDA Code of Conduct to protect impartiality.
Q83. How can an assessor create a supportive environment before assessment?
Answer guide: Make the setting suitable; welcome the candidate and build
rapport; allow time to feel comfortable and prepare; and invite questions.
